Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-11-22 15:00 UTC

Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Nina Park (Redwood Solutions), Liam O'Connor (NovaScale), Priya Rao (NovaScale), Marcus Li (NovaScale SRE), Hannah Vu (Product)

[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Liam: Yeah Liam here, Priya's on, Marcus is on as well. Thanks, Samira.
[00:10] Diego: Diego from Redwood, SE. I'll drive the tech parts.
[00:13] Priya: Priya here. We got a couple of failing cases we flagged in the ticket.
[00:18] Samira: Cool. Goal for today: understand the pattern of the regressions when you switched to the INT8/AWQ stack, and map potential runtime mitigations.
[00:28] Liam: To be clear, we're running on prem, in our VPC, 3x A100s. We tried two variants: GPTQ-converted model and an AWQ run. AWQ was attractive for perf but we see higher endpoint drift.
[00:42] Diego: Got it. Can you remind us which model family and sequence lengths you're hitting?
[00:46] Priya: It's close to LLaMA-3-Chat style, 16k context sometimes, but most calls are 2k to 4k. A lot of prefix caching for convo state.
[00:55] Nina: Quick clarification — when you say drift: is it semantic hallucination, or token-level probability shifts leading to formatting changes?
[01:02] Priya: Mostly content-level shifts, like word-choice and occasional missing qualifiers in legal-ese prompts. The correctness bar is high.
[01:08] Marcus: And it's intermittent, which makes it worse. Some requests are fine, others subtly off.
[01:12] Diego: Intermittent sounds like either layer non-determinism post-quant or an interaction with KV-cache warmup and batching. We'll want to correlate request timing and KV hit-rate.
[01:21] Samira: We'll run per-layer diffs, but I'd like to talk through hypotheses. Diego, can you walk the team through known AWQ/INT8 failure modes?
[01:28] Diego: Sure. High level: GPTQ tends to preserve distribution if calibrated well, but can be slow. AWQ is faster, and often uses aggressive block quant or asymmetric scale per-row, which helps throughput but can amplify outliers in certain attention heads. INT8 path can flip rare tokens if small layers with high dynamic range are quantized improperly.
[01:47] Priya: We suspected attention heads being brittle — we saw large logit shifts when a particular prompt pattern hits a narrow prefix.
[01:55] Diego: That's consistent. Also FP8 (experimental) can sometimes be a middle ground — better dynamic range than INT8 but requires runtime support; we have a lab build but haven't run on customer's infra yet.
[02:04] Liam: We can't deploy experimental kernels to prod yet, but for a bench it's okay.
[02:08] Samira: Important bit: on-prem network noise can also affect perceived intermittent failures if you're seeing cold KV misses, which trigger different execution paths. Marcus, can you describe your KV cache topology?
[02:18] Marcus: Sure. Each GPU has local KV shards, but we use a leader to sync prefix state for long-running sessions. Cold calls generate a lot of cache misses in the first 10 tokens until the session warms.
[02:30] Diego: That's exactly a path divergence — warm-KV uses cached past key/val and skips some recompute; cold-KV triggers the full decoding stack. If your quantized kernels have slightly different rounding, that can compound over long seqs.
[02:45] Hannah: So we might only see issues after warmup or only on cold start? Which is worse?
[02:49] Priya: We've seen both. Sometimes cold-starts align with drift, sometimes after long sessions (KV staleness?)
[02:56] Diego: There are two separate phenomena: warmup error accumulation and stale KV coherence. We need to instrument both. We'll add micro-benchmarks that replay realistic session patterns.
[03:08] Samira: Let's sketch an experiment matrix: INT8-gptq, INT8-awq, fp8-awq, baseline fp16. Test cold-start, warm-run, and variable batch sizes (1, 4, 16). Diego?
[03:20] Diego: Yep, and add 'sticky-KV' case where the client re-uses same session across different model variants to detect divergence. Also log per-step token probs for diffs.
[03:30] Priya: How expensive is per-step probing? It could add perf overhead.
[03:33] Diego: It's lightweight for benching — not for prod. We'll record token logits for 200 prompts and compute n-gram diff stats.
[03:40] Liam: That should surface layer-level sensitivity. How do you do layer-probing?
[03:44] Diego: We insert a probe after each transformer block to capture hidden state norms and compare against fp16 baseline. We look for layers where the L2 norm deviation spikes.
[03:52] Priya: If a layer spikes, what are remediation options?
[03:55] Diego: Options: per-layer selective dequant (keep that layer in fp16/FP32), layerwise bias correction, or runtime precision gating (if we detect the pattern, swap that layer to higher precision for the request).
[04:06] Samira: We call that 'precision gating' — switch code path at runtime with minimal latency hit. Diego, any numbers?
[04:12] Diego: In our internal tests, gating one or two layers to fp16 increased latency by ~8-12% but restored accuracy in most cases. Better than full fp16 cost.
[04:20] Marcus: The gating requires fast kernel fallback. Do we have runtime stability in our on-prem kernels? We've seen occasional kernel timeouts under batch churn.
[04:27] Diego: We're aware — we'll instrument kernel-level fallback metrics. Also propose a small warmup schedule for batch bursts to stabilize kernels.
[04:34] Hannah: How about batching? Our throughput needs mean we often batch to 8 or 16. But users care about tail latency.
[04:40] Diego: There's a latency vs throughput tradeoff. With quantized kernels, batching tends to amortize quant overhead, but it can increase the chance of cache-coherence events. For critical flows, use smaller batches + sticky-KV affinity to keep latency low and KV hit-rate high.
[04:54] Priya: We're also locked into a managed firewall policy — some calls get sporadic jitter due to ACL re-evals. Could network jitter cause accuracy differences?
[05:02] Diego: Not directly, but network jitter can change request timing and thus whether the KV-cache was warm; that changes execution path which might surface quantization differences. It's an indirect coupling.
[05:12] Samira: Good note. This is why we suggested collecting request timestamps and KV-hit metrics.
[05:18] Liam: On GPTQ vs AWQ: GPTQ preserves more fidelity usually, but we've seen AWQ match GPTQ on many ws tasks. Where AWQ diverges, can it be fixed by per-channel scale tweaks?
[05:29] Diego: Often yes. AWQ parameterization (block size, scale granularity) is tunable. We can sweep those knobs for suspect layers. Also consider hybrid-quant: GPTQ for attention-heavy layers and AWQ elsewhere.
[05:41] Priya: That sounds promising. Does Redwood runtime support hybrid per-layer quant selection?
[05:44] Diego: Yes, our runtime accepts a per-layer profile; we can roll out a per-deploy profile. For on-prem, we'll need the mapping file and to ensure kernels for both quant schemes exist.
[05:55] Marcus: Are kernels binary-compatible across our infra? We're locked to a specific CUDA driver rev.
[05:59] Diego: We'll validate. If driver mismatch occurs, we'll offer a compatibility matrix and fallback builds.
[06:05] Hannah: Can you explain the FP8 pilot? What's the practical upside?
[06:09] Diego: FP8 offers better dynamic range than INT8 and smaller memory than FP16. On some layers it reduces quant-induced bias. But kernel support and determinism are still experimental; for benching it's fine.
[06:22] Priya: We must ensure auditability and reproducibility for legal prompts. Does FP8 make audits harder?
[06:27] Diego: Slightly — more variance at tail tokens in some vendors' FP8 builds, so we'll provide deterministic seeds and logging for audit trails.
[06:34] Samira: Let's talk about regression detection: what thresholds should trigger fallback?
[06:38] Diego: We typically use token-level KL divergence + downstream metric drop (like top-1 accuracy on eval prompts). Set conservative thresholds for prod; for pilot set them lower to capture signals.
[06:48] Priya: Example numbers?
[06:49] Diego: In our experience, KL > 0.15 at token-level correlates with user-visible drift on legal text. But we'll calibrate to your eval set.
[06:58] Liam: Oh, and one other: audit logs and SSO. We'll need SAML in the on-prem control plane.
[07:04] Samira: Yes, Redwood Private supports SAML/KMS integrations — Samira to share specifics after this call.
[07:10] Nina: Back to runtime: Diego, can you detail how we'll implement probing without impacting perf?
[07:14] Diego: We'll use sample-based probes: 1% of requests in bench env, full capture for curated 200 prompt set. For production, probes are off by default; toggles via console.
[07:24] Marcus: For the on-prem bench, we can open a narrow test window with traffic replay. We'll mirror traffic to bench cluster.
[07:30] Priya: We'll share failing examples right after the call.
[07:33] Diego: Great. We'll start with per-layer L2 norm deltas and token-level KL histograms. We'll send you a sample output format so you can verify it's capturing what you need.
[07:43] Samira: Quick risk recap: major unknowns are driver/kernel compatibility, FP8 determinism, and how much latency precision gating costs in your SLA.
[07:52] Liam: Acceptable — we're okay with a small latency hit if accuracy is restored.
[07:56] Priya: Any quick wins to try before the bench?
[07:59] Diego: Easiest: enable sticky-KV session affinity and lower batch size for the problematic endpoints. Also rollback to GPTQ for the small percentage of sessions where you saw the worst drift.
[08:10] Marcus: We'll test sticky-KV and batch size changes this week.
[08:13] Samira: Great. I'll circulate the checklist and timeline.
[08:17] Hannah: One last question — do you have prescriptive thresholds for when to prefer AWQ vs GPTQ?
[08:22] Diego: Yes, we generally prefer GPTQ for high-regulatory/precision workloads (legal, finance), AWQ for chatty, latency-sensitive flows. Hybrid is common. We'll codify a short rubric.
[08:34] Liam: Thanks. That rubric will help our rollout decisions.
